title: Question 6
stem:
Fig. 6.1 shows part of a bridge rectifier circuit that can be used for rectification of an alternating input voltage $V_{IN}$.

{{figure:figure_6_1}}

Fig. 6.1

The circuit contains four diodes, one of which is shown.
The rectified output voltage $V_{OUT}$ is applied across load resistor R.

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: State what is meant by rectification.
hints: Hint 1: Think about what kind of current goes into the bridge and what kind you want across the load resistor R - what changes about direction of flow?
parts.proper_answer: Rectification is the conversion of an alternating current (a.c.) to a direct current (d.c.).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What a.c. and d.c. mean**
Think of a.c. as current that keeps reversing direction, so the voltage alternates positive and negative. Think of d.c. as current in one direction only, so the voltage stays the same sign.

Step 2: **Putting it together**
Rectification uses diodes to allow current one way only, so the alternating input is turned into a unidirectional output. That is conversion of a.c. to d.c.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: State the name of the type of rectification produced by a bridge rectifier circuit.
hints: Hint 1: Think about whether a bridge with four diodes uses just one half of the a.c. cycle or both halves to make output humps.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Half-wave versus full-wave**
A single diode passes only one half of the cycle and blocks the other, which is half-wave. A bridge steers both the positive and negative halves so both give a forward output.

Step 2: **Name for bridge action**
Because both halves of the input appear as output, this is called full-wave rectification.

hints: Hint 1: Focus on the load resistor R - the current through it must always go the same way (top to bottom) on both halves of the input cycle, so work out which bridge arms must conduct on each half.
Hint 2: Use the diode already drawn as a guide - it points left, so follow how current must loop from input, through R, and back to complete the bridge diamond.
parts.proper_answer: Three diode symbols drawn in the dashed circles to complete the bridge diamond. Lower-left diode points to the right, upper-left and lower-right diodes both point to the left, giving unidirectional current through R.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Rule for the bridge**
You sitting beside me, remember the golden rule: current through R is always downwards. The diodes act as one-way valves to steer the a.c. input so that happens on both positive and negative half-cycles.

Step 2: **Matching the given diode**
The diode shown on the top-right points to the left, toward the top of R. To make a closed loop, the top-left diode must also point left toward the top of R, the bottom-left diode must point right toward the bottom common point, and the bottom-right diode must point left toward the bottom common point. Draw all three with the standard triangle-and-bar symbol inside the dashed circles.

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem:
The input voltage varies with time $t$ according to the equation

$$V_{IN} = 34 \sin 18t$$

where $V_{IN}$ is in $\text{V}$ and $t$ is in $\text{s}$.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: Show that the period of the input voltage is $0.35\text{ s}$.
hints: Hint 1: Look at the form $V_{IN} = 34 \sin 18t$ and compare with the standard sine form $V_0 \sin \omega t$ - what physical quantity does the number 18 represent?
Hint 2: Recall how that quantity is linked to period $T$ for one full oscillation, then substitute the value to check $T$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Identify angular frequency**
The standard form is: $$V = V_0 \sin \omega t$$ Comparing with $$V_{IN} = 34 \sin 18t$$ gives peak $V_0 = 34 \text{ V}$ and $$\omega = 18 \text{ rad s}^{-1}$$

Step 2: **Convert to period**
One cycle corresponds to $2\pi$ radians, so: $$T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega} = \frac{2\pi}{18}$$ $$T = 0.349 \text{ s} \approx 0.35 \text{ s}$$ This shows the required value.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Think about how the heating effect of a sine wave compares to its peak - the r.m.s. value is smaller than the 34 V peak by a fixed square-averaging factor.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Peak to r.m.s. for a sine**
For a sinusoidal voltage, the r.m.s. value is the peak divided by $\sqrt{2}$: $$V_{r.m.s.} = \frac{V_0}{\sqrt{2}}$$

Step 2: **Substitute**
Here $V_0 = 34 \text{ V}$, so: $$V_{r.m.s.} = \frac{34}{\sqrt{2}} = 24 \text{ V}$$ to 2 s.f.

hints: Hint 1: Think about what full-wave does to negative halves of the input sine - do they disappear or are they flipped to become positive humps?
Hint 2: Think about the peak height of $V_{OUT}$ compared to the 34 V peak of $V_{IN}$, and whether $V_{OUT}$ can ever go negative.
Hint 3: Think about how many output humps fit into one 0.35 s input period, and at what times $V_{OUT}$ must touch zero.
parts.proper_answer: Sketch shows two positive (or two negative) sinusoidal humps from 0 to 0.35 s, minimum 0 V, peak 34 V, with zeros at $t = 0$, 0.175 s and 0.350 s.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Shape - flipped humps**
Full-wave keeps both halves but makes them the same sign. So you do not get a full sine, you get repeated humps above zero (all positive is fine, all negative is also accepted if consistent). Minimum is $0 \text{ V}$ where the input crosses zero.

Step 2: **Peak value**
Ideal diodes drop no voltage, so the output peak equals the input peak: $$V_{OUT,peak} = 34 \text{ V}$$ Draw each hump up to 34 V on the $V_{OUT}$ axis.

Step 3: **Timing - twice the frequency**
One input period 0.35 s gives two output humps. So zeros at start, middle and end: $$t = 0, \quad t = 0.175 \text{ s}, \quad t = 0.350 \text{ s}$$ with smooth sine-shaped humps in between, spanning $t = 0$ to $t = 0.35 \text{ s}$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.part_stem: Resistor R has a resistance of $56\text{ k}\Omega$. A capacitor of capacitance $12\mu\text{F}$ is connected into the circuit of Fig. 6.1 in order to smooth the output voltage.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.text: On Fig. 6.1, draw the capacitor correctly connected into the circuit.

markscheme_points.text: correct circuit symbol for capacitor, connected in parallel with resistor

hints: Hint 1: Think about where a reservoir capacitor must sit so it can charge up when $V_{OUT}$ is high and then discharge through R when $V_{OUT}$ tries to fall.
parts.proper_answer: Capacitor symbol drawn in parallel with resistor R, connected across the two output terminals.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Job of smoothing**
The capacitor stores charge on the peak and releases it when the rectified voltage falls, filling in the gaps. To do that it must see the same voltage as R.

Step 2: **Correct place**
So connect the capacitor directly across R, one plate to the top output node and one plate to the bottom output node, in parallel with R.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: Calculate the time constant of the smoothing circuit.
hints: Hint 1: Think about which two component values control how slowly the smoothing capacitor discharges through the load.
Hint 2: Check the units carefully - convert $k\Omega$ to $\Omega$ and $\mu F$ to $F$ before multiplying.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Formula for time constant**
Discharge through a resistor is governed by: $$\tau = RC$$ A large $R$ or large $C$ means slower decay and better smoothing.

Step 2: **Numbers with conversions**
$$R = 56 \text{ k}\Omega = 56 \times 10^3 \text{ }\Omega$$ $$C = 12 \text{ }\mu\text{F} = 12 \times 10^{-6} \text{ F}$$ $$\tau = 56 \times 10^3 \times 12 \times 10^{-6} = 0.672 \text{ s} \approx 0.67 \text{ s}$$

parts.label: (c)(iii)
parts.text:
During each discharge cycle, the time for which the capacitor is discharging is $0.14\text{ s}$.

Determine the minimum value of the smoothed output voltage.
hints: Hint 1: Think about the starting voltage at the top of a hump and the discharge time given - which exponential decay law links voltage to time and time constant?
Hint 2: Identify $V_0$, $t$ and $\tau$ from the question and previous part, then evaluate the decay over 0.14 s.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Decay from the peak**
During discharge the capacitor voltage falls exponentially from the 34 V peak: $$V = V_0 e^{-t/\tau}$$ Here $V_0 = 34 \text{ V}$, discharge time $t = 0.14 \text{ s}$, and $\tau = 0.67 \text{ s}$ from (c)(ii).

Step 2: **Calculate minimum**
$$V_{min} = 34 \exp\left(-\frac{0.14}{0.67}\right)$$ $$V_{min} = 34 \times 0.811 \approx 28 \text{ V}$$ This is the lowest voltage before the next hump recharges the capacitor.
